name: Iranian Publishers
description: Iranian publishers connect original writing, translation, scholarship, illustration, and reading communities. Historical publishing houses and contemporary specialist imprints show how editorial choices shape the books available to readers.

seo.title: Iranian Publishers: Editorial Traditions and Specialist Imprints | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian publishing through Amir Kabir, contemporary literary publishing, children's books, and the people who select and translate texts.

content.heading: Publishers as cultural intermediaries
content.content:
A publisher's contribution begins before a book reaches a printing press. Research on Iranian translation describes a network of publishers, translators, editors, and informal advisers who help determine which foreign texts become available in Persian. Anthropologist Hosna Sheikholeslami calls attention to the *ketab shenass*, or “book knower”: a reputation-based adviser whose recommendations can influence publishers and translators. Her research primarily concerns Tehran and fieldwork in 2012–2014; it should not be read as a census of the entire industry. [s1]

This perspective makes publishing more than a list of company names. The selection of a manuscript, the choice of a translator, and the development of a recognizable catalogue all help shape intellectual exchange. Formal job titles capture only part of that work. [s1]

content.heading: Amir Kabir and the growth of an editorial institution
content.content:
Amir Kabir offers a particularly well-documented historical example. Abdolrahim Jafari founded the publishing house in Tehran in 1949. Its development included an editorial department, payments to authors and translators, and specialist subsidiaries for different readerships. The catalogue brought Persian literary selections, translated educational writing, and substantial reference works into the same publishing enterprise. [s2]

The Mo'in Persian dictionary illustrates the sustained editorial investment behind such projects: its publication extended from 1963 to 1973. These reference works belonged to a different production rhythm from a single novel or pamphlet. Following the 1979 revolution, Amir Kabir was confiscated by court order and transferred to the Organization for the Promotion of Islam. Its earlier history therefore cannot be treated as evidence of uninterrupted ownership or editorial policy. [s2]

content.heading: Different catalogues, different audiences
content.content:
Contemporary publisher websites reveal distinctions that a general label such as “Iranian books” can conceal. Cheshmeh's publishing site presents individual works alongside facilities for manuscript submission and copyright-related enquiries. Its wider cultural network separately identifies publishing imprints, bookselling, and distribution. These are connected activities, but they are not interchangeable functions. [s3][s4]

Children's publishing offers another route into the field. Tehran-based TUTI identifies itself as the children's and young-adult division of Fatemi Publishing. Its English-language catalogue presents picture books and named creators, making the publisher's work accessible to readers and professionals who do not read Persian. This establishes its stated specialization; it does not independently measure its market share or international reach. [s5]

For an international reader, the most useful starting point is therefore the individual edition: its author, translator, illustrator where relevant, and publishing imprint. A publisher's catalogue can reveal an editorial direction, while a corporate description alone cannot establish the quality of every title. The examples here introduce several publishing functions without claiming to rank the sector.

name: Bookshops
description: Iranian bookshops connect readers with publishers, editions, translators, and literary discussion. Selected historical and contemporary examples show how bookselling overlaps with publishing, cultural programming, and online retail.

seo.title: Bookshops in Iran: Bookselling and Reading Culture | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover how Iranian bookselling connects editions, publishers, readers, cultural events, and online catalogues, with carefully sourced examples.

content.heading: Where publishing meets the reader
content.content: The history of Amir Kabir shows how closely publishing and bookselling could develop together. Its founder, Abdolrahim Jafari, established the publishing business on Tehran's Naser Khosrow Avenue, opened a nearby bookstore, and subsequently expanded its retail presence. A publishing house could thus participate directly in the encounter between a reader and its books. This is a historical example, not a description of every Iranian publisher's business model. [s1]

content.heading: The knowledge behind a recommendation
content.content:
Bookselling involves more than locating a title. In ethnographic observations at the Tehran International Book Fair in 2013, Hosna Sheikholeslami describes conversations about translators, reprints, publication history, and differences between editions. Some exchanges supplied information without producing a sale. Her account also distinguishes expertise directed toward customers from the advice that informal “book knowers” offer publishers and translators. [s2]

These observations help explain why the identity of an edition matters. Two books bearing the same translated title may require further comparison: the translator, publisher, and printing history can be important parts of the reader's choice. This is an interpretation grounded in the study's examples, rather than a claim that all editions differ or that all booksellers provide equivalent advice. The research describes particular relationships and encounters, not a nationwide service standard. [s2]

content.heading: Retail, catalogues, and cultural conversation
content.content:
Cheshmeh's online bookshop illustrates the range of activities that can sit around a bookselling identity. Its website distinguishes the online shop from named physical branches and organizes books alongside stationery, gifts, and games. It also offers reading pathways around authors and subjects. The catalogue therefore provides both products and an editorial way of navigating them. These website categories establish the retailer's presentation, not the stock or opening hours of a particular branch. [s3]

A different example comes from Shahr-e Ketab, usually rendered in English as Book City. Its cultural department presents lectures, meetings, courses, interviews, and audiovisual material. The department dates its programme of cultural, literary, and philosophical meetings to Azar 1384 in the Iranian Solar Hijri calendar. Its published material includes discussions of classical Persian literature and translated writing. [s4]

This cultural programme should not be assumed to operate identically at every shop carrying the Book City name. The evidence concerns the cultural department and its published activities. Nevertheless, it shows how a bookselling-associated institution can create occasions for readers to discuss books with authors, translators, and other participants. [s4]

Together, these examples suggest several ways to understand a bookshop: a point of sale, a guide through competing editions, and a setting for literary exchange. They remain an introduction rather than a directory. A useful national account also needs evidence from independent shops, second-hand sellers, and communities beyond Tehran.

name: Tehran International Book Fair
description: The Tehran International Book Fair combines public book sales with cultural programming and professional publishing exchanges. Its 2025 edition included physical and online purchasing as well as a fellowship programme intended to advance translations of Iranian books.

seo.title: Tehran International Book Fair: Readers, Publishers and Rights | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand the Tehran International Book Fair's public sales, international section, and translation exchanges through documented 2025 activities.

content.heading: A fair for readers and publishing professionals
content.content:
The Tehran International Book Fair brings public purchasing and professional exchange into the same event. Its official introduction emphasizes direct book sales and identifies Iran Book and Literature House as the organizer commissioned by the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance. This institutional description explains the fair's stated remit; its promotional claims about cultural importance are not independent measurements of impact. [s2]

The official website provides separate routes for exhibitor registration, book and publisher searches, news, and international participation. These functions help distinguish the fair from a simple retail sale: publishers and cultural institutions can also use it to present catalogues and establish professional contacts. [s1][s3]

content.heading: What the 2025 evidence establishes
content.content:
The official international-section rules specify May 7–17, 2025. Contemporary reporting by WANA gives the same dates for the 36th edition and identifies the venue as the Imam Khomeini Mosalla, a large religious and exhibition complex in Tehran. WANA also describes an online purchasing channel operating alongside the physical fair. The venue name identifies the location; it does not make every book or programme religious in subject. [s3][s4]

A separate official fellowship report gives May 6–16 in its closing paragraph. Because that conflicts with both the participation rules and contemporary reporting, the dates should be treated as an editorial discrepancy in the official material. This page uses May 7–17 for the documented edition and does not extrapolate a future timetable from it. [s3][s4][s5]

content.heading: International participation has several purposes
content.content:
The 2025 rules describe an international section open to several kinds of participants, including foreign book fairs, embassies and cultural institutions, international organizations, literary agencies, and publishers involved in translating Persian titles or selling rights abroad. Consequently, “international participation” can refer to cultural representation, professional negotiation, or book display rather than a single uniform activity. [s3]

Participation also operates within explicit restrictions. The rules prohibit exhibiting, selling, or distributing works banned in Iran and require advance notice to the hall manager for a forum. These provisions establish formal conditions for that section; they do not document every decision made during the event. [s3]

content.heading: From a meeting to a translated book
content.content:
An official report dated May 15, 2025 describes the first publishing-industry fellowship and workshops devoted to children's and young-adult books. A ministry official reported that Iranian titles had reached a pre-contract stage in several languages, with further review by the Grant Scheme Secretariat still required. [s5]

That distinction is essential. A discussion, preliminary agreement, finalized contract, and published translation are different outcomes. The report supports the existence of negotiations and professional programming; it does not establish that every proposed translation subsequently appeared. The fair can therefore be understood as a meeting point in the publishing process, while its lasting effects require evidence beyond announcements made during the event. [s5]
